claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr forms a high density of short-range-order clusters at approximately 1000 °C.
Atomic-size and modulus mismatches among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr cause the proposed short-range order.
The SRO clusters reversibly pin gliding dislocations.
Reversible dislocation pinning increases the storage of mobile dislocations.
The proposed dislocation interactions sustain work hardening.
Sustained work hardening retards strain localization.
At 1000 °C, WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain and toughness than pure tungsten under otherwise identical tensile conditions.
The proposed SRO clusters are approximately 1–2 nm in size.
The proposed SRO-cluster density is at least 10^23 m^-3.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit at least 1.5 times the uniform elongation of pure tungsten at 1000 °C.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit at least 1.5 times the toughness of pure tungsten at 1000 °C.
The area under a tensile stress–strain curve is identified as fracture toughness.
The hypothesis applies for grain sizes of 10–30 µm, temperatures of 900–1100 °C, strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1, and oxygen contents below 1000 ppm.
Matching the alloy and tungsten to a grain size of 20±5 µm and impurity levels below 500 ppm is part of the proposed controlled comparison.
Both materials will be tensile-tested at 1000 °C and an engineering strain rate of 1×10^-3 s^-1 with identical geometry and thermomechanical pretreatment.
High vacuum below 10^-5 Torr or an inert-gas environment suppresses oxidation during testing.

contradictions.description: The intervention says testing stops at the onset of necking, but the outcome and measurements require an area under the stress–strain curve described as fracture toughness. Stopping at necking does not provide the complete deformation-to-fracture curve needed for a total tensile-toughness measure, and a tensile-curve integral is not itself a standard fracture-toughness measurement.
